name: Vistry Group PLC
executive_summary: Vistry Group is the UK’s largest volume housebuilder by completions, running a partner-funded mixed-tenure model (74% of FY2025 completions pre-sold to registered providers, local authorities and the PRS). The quantitative screen rates the shares a strong buy, which is consistent with a still-profitable franchise whose returns and reported earnings were reset by the 2024 South Division cost-forecasting failure and which is now trading through a working-capital-heavy recovery. FY2025 adjusted profit before tax edged up to £268.8m (2024: £263.5m) on 15,658 completions (2024: 17,225), while reported profit before tax recovered to £196.2m (2024: £104.9m) and year-end net debt fell to £144.2m. The debate is whether the partnerships land bank, Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) alignment and year-end deleveraging outweigh open-market cyclicality, a 13.9% ROCE versus a 40% medium-term target, elevated average daily debt, combined Chair/CEO governance, and control-quality scars that a value screen does not capture. `screening_snapshot.json` is not in this pack, so model-level cheapness metrics cannot be verified here.
investment_thesis:
For a value investor the strong-buy screen is a cyclical asset-and-earnings reset: a scaled UK partnerships developer with visible partner-funded volumes, a large owned and controlled land bank (71,501 plots at 31 December 2025) and modest year-end net debt relative to the equity and inventory the business carries. That is the quality hook that typically supports deep-value and financial-health models, even when reported ROCE is depressed.

The screen file itself is missing, so this overlay uses only the stated strong-buy signal, not a reconstructed P/E, P/B or model-pass list. Filing evidence that supports a value case: the Group delivered one in seven of the country’s affordable homes in FY2025; partner-funded completions were 11,593 (74% of the total); more than 150 new partner agreements were signed with over 65 counterparties; Vistry Works delivered a record 4,643 timber-frame units (2024: 2,900); and the Board is targeting a year-end net cash position in 2026 after cutting net debt by £36.5m in FY2025. Structural demand support cited in the 2025 annual report includes the SAHP (described as a £39bn June announcement and as £37bn in November 2025 bidding guidance), a £50m allocation from £2bn of affordable top-up funding, a CPI+1% rent settlement from April 2026, and the PlacePoint joint venture with Homes England (£150m available capital; first site transferred in December 2025).

What the screen cannot see, and what therefore caps conviction, is that this is not yet a high-quality compounder on the Group’s own targets. Adjusted operating profit was £353.8m on adjusted revenue of £4,155.3m in FY2025 (implied margin about 8.5% versus a 12% medium-term target); ROCE was 13.9% (2024: 14.6%; 2023 restated: 20.9%); and average daily debt rose to £734m (2024: £698m). FY2024 also restated 2023 profits after a forensic review of South Division cost forecasting. The strong-buy signal is therefore coherent with cheapness after an earnings collapse, but only partially confirmed as a quality franchise until group interim trading, covenant detail and the missing screen snapshot can be checked.
financial_review:
Primary source: Companies House body extracts. `filings_index.json` (regime `uk_rns`) labels all seven items `period: other` (annual 0, interim 0). In substance the bodies include four group annual reports (FY2022–FY2025) and one unaudited parent-company interim; there are no consolidated group half-year results and no RNS trading updates in the index. `financials_annual.json` is not in the pack; no Yahoo fallback was used. All figures below are from filing extracts.

Annual results — FY2022 (Annual Report 2022, Companies House 8 June 2023).
Adjusted revenue £3,073.2m (2021: £2,693.6m); adjusted profit before tax £418.4m (2021: £346.0m); adjusted basic EPS 137.5p. Reported revenue £2,729.4m; reported profit before tax £247.5m after exceptional expenses of £153.9m, including a £97.0m fire-safety provision and £56.9m of transaction and integration costs. Completions in the following year’s report: 11,951. Year-end net cash £118.2m is given as the FY2022 comparative in the 2023 annual report. Fire-safety provision £309.2m at 31 December 2022.

Annual results — FY2023 (Annual Report 2023, Companies House 28 May 2024; subsequently restated).
As originally reported: adjusted revenue £4,042.1m; adjusted operating profit £487.9m; adjusted profit before tax £419.1m; adjusted basic EPS 88.2p; reported revenue £3,564.2m; reported operating profit £311.8m; reported profit before tax £304.8m; reported EPS 64.6p; completions 16,118; owned and controlled plots 76,434; ROCE 21.3% (2022: 25.0%); net debt £88.8m (down from £328.7m at 30 June 2023). Exceptional expenses £65.6m (integration/restructuring £46.3m; fire safety/second staircase £19.3m). Fire-safety provision £289.0m at 31 December 2023; Developer Remediation Contract signed 13 March 2023; Residential Property Developer Tax described as about 4% of relevant profits (c. £20.2m paid to date in that report). Strategy: exclusive Partnerships model from September 2023; medium-term 40% ROCE; £1bn of capital distributions targeted through FY2026.

The 2024 annual report restated 2023 comparatives for South Division cost-forecasting error: adjusted operating profit £476.1m; adjusted profit before tax £407.3m; adjusted EPS 85.8p; reported operating profit £300.0m; reported profit before tax £293.0m; reported EPS 62.1p; ROCE 20.9%. Use restated 2023 figures for trend; the original 2023 report overstated profit.

Annual results — FY2024 (Annual Report 2024, Companies House 10 June 2025).
A sharp down-year. Adjusted revenue £4,329.2m; adjusted operating profit £358.2m; adjusted profit before tax £263.5m (2023 restated: £407.3m); adjusted EPS 55.9p. Reported revenue £3,779.3m; reported operating profit £167.0m; reported profit before tax £104.9m; reported EPS 22.0p. Completions 17,225 (+7%); mix 73% partner-funded / 27% open market; partner-funded units 12,633 (+18%); open-market units 4,592 (−15%); sales rate 1.07 per site per week. ROCE 14.6%. On 8 October 2024 the Group disclosed understated full-life costs in the South Division: 18 sites needed adjustments of more than £1m; five large sites accounted for 60% of the movement; total cost adjustments £165m, of which £91.5m hit 2024 adjusted profit before tax and £53m falls in future years; a further £8m adjusted-PBT reduction came from CVR reviews in the other 22 regions. An independent forensic review reported to the Audit Committee Chair attributed the issues to insufficient management capability, non-compliant commercial forecasting and poor divisional culture, confined to the former housebuilding South Division. No final ordinary distribution for 2024; remaining H1 2024 ordinary (£55m) and special (£75m) distributions to be completed by buyback. Indebtedness was “higher than expected”; FY2025 priority was cash generation. Year-end net debt is not in the extracted 2024 highlights; the FY2025 report gives £180.7m at 30 December 2024.

Annual results — FY2025 (Annual Report 2025, Companies House 25 June 2026; Chair’s statement dated 3 March 2026).
Stabilisation, not a full recovery. Adjusted revenue £4,155.3m (cover table; narrative £4.2bn versus £4.3bn); adjusted operating profit £353.8m; adjusted profit before tax £268.8m (+2%); adjusted EPS 59.3p. Reported revenue £3,613.7m; reported operating profit £222.6m; reported profit before tax £196.2m; reported EPS 42.2p. Completions 15,658 (−9%); ASP +3% to £282k; partner-funded 11,593 (−8%), 74% of completions; open market 4,065 (−11%); PRS volumes −23% and 18% of completions (2024: 21%); sales rate 0.96 (2024: 1.07). Land sales £180m of revenue (FY2024: £91m). Net debt £144.2m (inflow £36.5m versus 2024 outflow £91.9m); average daily debt £734m (2024: £698m), above target because of delayed partner-funded deals and slower inventory reduction. Land replenishment 12,599 plots on 44 sites (c. 9,500 plots on 30 sites in H2), including Worcester, Rugeley and Bury St Edmunds (c. 5,000 plots combined); strategic land bank 76,368 plots. ROCE 13.9%. Medium-term targets unchanged: ~20,000 units of divisional capacity, 40% ROCE and 12% adjusted operating margin. Capital allocation: £29m of the existing buyback still to run in 2026, then distributions to be reviewed; highest near-term priority is lower capital employed and a net cash year-end with “much reduced” H2 average daily debt. Build-cost inflation described as low single-digit in 2025, with “minimal” material and labour inflation expected in 2026 subject to geopolitics. Going-concern and viability statements are listed at page 83 of the 2025 report (page 76 of the 2024 report), but the extracted bodies do not include the statement text, covenant headroom or facility amounts — a material gap.

Interim — parent company only, six months to 30 June 2024 (unaudited, filed 12 September 2024 under CA 2006 s838 to evidence distributable reserves).
These are not group results. Parent profit before tax £237.8m, almost entirely £250.0m subsidiary dividend income less £18.5m finance costs. Parent net assets £2,528.7m; borrowings £496.5m; cash £151.9m; distributable profits £394.8m after treating the full £100m buyback announced 14 March 2024 as a reduction in reserves (£50.5m actually repurchased by 30 June). Cannot be used to infer consolidated H1 2024 or any later group trading. No H1 2025 or H1 2026 group interim is in the index.
risks_and_flags:
Accounting and controls. The 2024 South Division episode is the principal red flag a quantitative screen will under-weight: restated 2023 profits, £165m of full-life cost adjustments, forensic findings of non-compliant CVRs and weak culture, plus £8m of smaller adjustments outside that division. The 2025 report says Investment Committee, CVR and commercial-assurance changes are now “firmly embedded”, but the extracts do not provide a clean audit-committee quantification of residual risk, and recurrence through a full cycle is unproven.

Governance and key person. Greg Fitzgerald has been combined Executive Chair and CEO since the 2024 AGM; the Board acknowledges this departs from the UK Corporate Governance Code. SID Rob Woodward has enhanced duties and “has led the development of the CEO succession plan” for a transition “when the time comes” — timing is not specified. Earl Sibley (COO) left at end-2024 when the COO role was removed. Sue Farr joined the Board in October 2025. Employee engagement and turnover deteriorated after the 2024 disruption (voluntary turnover 18.6% versus 15.4% at December 2024); the CultureAmp “favourable” scores in the extract are OCR-garbled and should be treated as unverified.

Cyclical and competitive. Open-market volumes and sales rates are still under mortgage-affordability pressure; PRS paused in 2025; partner-funded activity was delayed around the Autumn Budget. The Group remains a volume competitor in a politically driven affordable-housing market; grant timing and RP balance-sheet capacity are external. Medium-term 12% margin / 40% ROCE targets are far from current delivery.

Regulatory. CMA housebuilding investigation concluded; in July 2025 Vistry and six other housebuilders offered voluntary commitments to support affordable-home construction. Fire-safety remediation under the Developer Remediation Contract remains a live obligation; the last extracted provision figure is £289.0m at 31 December 2023 — FY2024 and FY2025 extracts in this pack do not update it. RPDT continues. Second-staircase rules added £19.3m of cost in FY2023.

Leverage and liquidity. Year-end net debt is falling, but average daily debt of £734m and an inventory-heavy land bank mean intra-year liquidity is tighter than the year-end print. FY2024 already showed indebtedness exceeding expectations and distributions being paused. Facility size, covenant tests and going-concern wording are not in the extracted bodies.

Short interest. The Investegate short-register extract (indexed February 2025; positions in the body dated to July 2026) shows multiple active stakes above 0.5%, including Schonfeld Strategic Advisors (UK) LLP 2.44% and GLG Partners LP 2.24% (8 July 2026), plus Citadel, Two Sigma and others. That is sceptical institutional positioning, not a corporate announcement.

Pension. No defined-benefit deficit, surplus or IAS 19 numbers appear in the extracted bodies (only a 2022 ROCE footnote referring to a “retirement benefit asset”). Treat as a data gap, not a clearance.

RiskTags: regulatory, cyclical, governance, leverage, accounting, competitive, liquidity, key_person
news_highlights:
`news_manifest.json` is missing. Coverage in this pack is thin: only two Investegate-derived items sit in the filings index, plus events narrated inside the annual reports.

- “Vistry to deliver 2,300 homes in Rugeley” — 14 August 2025 (Reach/RNS): acquisition of the 139-hectare former Rugeley Power Station site from ENGIE, outline planning for 2,300 mixed-tenure homes (affordable, PRS, open market), school, riverside park and commercial space. Consistent with the FY2025 strategic-land comment on Worcester, Rugeley and Bury St Edmunds.
- “Vistry Group (VTY) Short Positions” — Investegate short-register page (index date 28 February 2025; body lists active positions through 9 July 2026): not a company RNS; documents elevated disclosed short interest as above.

Annual-report narrative (not a news manifest) also records: CMA voluntary commitments (July 2025); PlacePoint first site transfer (December 2025); SAHP bidding opened end-February 2026; Sue Farr appointed (October 2025); Earl Sibley departure (end-2024). Flag: there is no structured year of headlines with which to assess trading updates, profit warnings, M&A beyond Rugeley, or management change after the FY2025 report.
research_rationale: FY2022–FY2025 filings support the screen’s deep-value hook — a still-profitable partnerships housebuilder with falling year-end net debt and a large land bank — but the 2024 restatement, ROCE and margin far below target, elevated average daily debt, heavy short interest, and missing group interims, screen snapshot and news file mean deep research only partially confirms a strong-buy case.
